title: A Ceremonial Guard, a Koopa Who Was Never Locked In, and the Handshake Under Peach's Castle — 955 BF
subtitle: The archivist argues that the night was not a conspiracy discovered but a schedule observed — that every door the guard went through was opened for him by somebody with a key, and that the only thing in the account the Arrangement did not plan was the man holding the lantern
filed: 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — the night after the filing, at the desk, with the 955 drawer open and the Who Signed file on the floor because the desk ran out
summary: The capital file has argued about the Arrangement for fifteen years from a dead man's journal. This account gives it a corridor: an unlocked cell, a bored prisoner, a handshake, three hoods who said the Guild was already in place, and a chamberlain who told the Guild out loud whom to kill. I argue the night was not discovered — it was scheduled — and that the schedule's one error was a ceremonial guard it had already dismissed as furniture.
thesis:
The 955 drawer is open and the Who Signed file is on the floor beside my chair, because the desk ran out of surface at around eleven and I have not picked it up. On the blotter, squared, is the account — the guard's own order, the table's record of it, in my copy with my pencil in the margins — and on top of that, weighing nothing, is the one sheet from it that matters, which is the night posting: a name, a post, an hour. Everything else in the account is a man walking away from that sheet.

I want to say the uncomfortable thing first and argue it afterwards. Nobody discovered anything in Peach's Castle that night. A ceremonial guard did not uncover a plot; he was inside one, moving through it in the only direction the building allowed, and the plot had already decided he did not count. Every door he went through was unlocked by somebody who had a key. Every room he got lost in was a room doing something scheduled — a procession at one in the morning, a wall of heavy Toads, a boy being minded past midnight, a hood walking with purpose. The dungeon cell was unlocked for a visitor. The hall's applause was arranged by an orb that arrived on time. The kill order was given in a voice that expected to be obeyed and was.

So the reading I am putting my name under is this: the night is a *schedule*, and the account is the one document in this archive written by somebody the schedule forgot to include. That is why it is worth more than the journal. The journal was written by a man who knew what he was describing. This was written by a man who did not, and his not knowing is the only reason he is alive to have it taken down. *WAH! Fifteen years of arguing about handwriting, and the thing that breaks the file open is a Toad who could not find the ballroom.*

sections.heading: 'Oh. It's You.' Is a Man Checking a Clock
sections.sourceAnchor: *"So you finally came to free me —"* and then, looking at a ceremonial guard with a lantern and two Toads in corridor livery, *"— oh. It's you."*
sections.body:
I have the line under my thumb. Two dashes, one each side of the turn, and the table's record puts the pause between them exactly where a man's face changes. I have read it aloud twice, quietly, because it reads differently out loud: the first half rises, the second half drops, and the drop is not fear. It is disappointment. A prisoner who is afraid of an open door says *who are you.* This one said *oh.*

That *oh* is the first evidence in fifteen years that the Arrangement kept time. He was expecting somebody at an hour, and the lantern came early or late, and he could tell the difference by livery. He knew what a ceremonial guard looked like and knew it was not his appointment. A real prisoner does not have appointments. A real prisoner's cell is not standing the way a door stands when a key has been turned in it and left — the account's phrase, and it is a good one, because that is a door that has been *set* rather than opened.

I put the account down and pick up the Loyalist copy of the journal pages — the Who Signed file, the sheet with my old pencil cross beside *the positions were cleared.* I made that cross in Harvestide because I did not know what *positions* meant and wanted to come back to it. I have come back to it. A position is a cell with the lock already turned, a corridor with the escort already dead, a post with the guard already lectured off it. The journal, if it is his, describes a building being prepared. The *oh* is the sound the preparation makes when a piece of it that was not prepared walks in holding a lamp.

One more thing, and then I will leave the Koopa until the shop. The account says the escort fell dead *between one breath and the next,* with no blade and no sound, and that the lantern shook. Nobody in that cell was surprised but the Toads. *WAH! I have read it a dozen times looking for the second escort and I am starting to think the account is not hiding him. I think he was simply not worth recording to anybody but me, which is how I know the account is honest and how I know what the night thought of Toads.*

sections.heading: Nobody Invents Getting Lost Five Times — and Every Wrong Room Was Busy
sections.sourceAnchor: A ballroom rehearsing a procession, a wall of heavy Toads, the dining hall, a hood going the other way, a tower.
sections.body:
I have the castle plans out — my own, the ones under the Peach's Castle article, with the basements inked in the second colour because I added them later — and I have walked his route on them with the blunt end of the pencil. It is not a wandering route. He went looking for the brothers and the building gave him, in order, a ballroom, a corridor, a dining hall, another corridor and a tower, and at no point did it give him an exit. I can draw his night as one line. It bends five times and never crosses itself.

The credibility point first, because it is the one I keep making and nobody keeps hearing. A forged account of this night would have the guard see the handshake and leave. It would not have him back out of a ballroom because trumpets were being rehearsed at one in the morning. It would not have him decline to pass a wall of heavy Toads. It would not slow down, as this one does, at a dining hall where a small boy is up past midnight with a plate in front of him, and then — this is the sentence I believe above all the others — *he did not stop,* because he was a guard off his post in a room he had no business in, and because *a boy at a table with a maid is a boy who is fine.* A liar makes the father heroic. This father kept walking because he was embarrassed.

Now the harder point, which the credibility point hides. Every wrong room was doing something. Toads marching in formation for no race. Heavy Toads shoulder to shoulder across a passage, facing outward, not speaking — that is not a guard detail, that is a *cordon,* and a cordon faces the thing it is keeping people from. A hood walking with purpose toward the dungeon stair. A child kept up and fed in the one room with a door onto the service passages. The guard thought he was lost in a castle. He was walking the perimeter of an operation at one in the morning, and the operation's own staff kept turning him back toward its centre, until two of them walked him the last of the way.

I set the pencil down flat on the plans so it does not roll. The line it drew ends at a cell. It did not have to start at a lantern post for that to be true, but it did, and the night posting on top of the pile says who put the lantern there. *WAH! The building was not confusing. The building was staffed.*

sections.heading: 'I Have the Keys to Every Door' Is the Journal Speaking With a Mouth
sections.sourceAnchor: *"I have the keys to every door,"* he said. Not as a threat; as an inventory.
sections.body:
Two sheets, side by side, under the lamp. Left: the Loyalist copy of the journal — *the timing was arranged, the positions were cleared,* in a hand the Regency says is forged. Right: the account's second section — a Toad in a new suit, on the ceremonial route, telling a guard with a lantern that he has the keys to every door, and then telling him to *bask in his inferiority,* and walking on. I have put a ruler across the two so that *positions* and *keys* sit on the same line. They are the same sentence. One is written by a man describing what he did. The other is said by a man in the middle of doing it, to somebody he had decided would not remember.

I owe the reader the attribution argument in daylight, because I made it in the filing and I will not hide behind having made it. The account says *chancellor.* In 955 BF that word belonged to the son, who was already styled Chancellor and was in the building on Highsun 1 by his own file. I have filed the words against the father — Toadsworth the Elder, Royal Chamberlain — and here is the whole of my reasoning so that it can be taken apart: a new suit a month before the succession; the keys to every door, which in a palace is a chamberlain's inventory and not a chancellor's; and, later, the authority to give the Mages' Guild an order in public and have it obeyed. The son's file is a file of memoranda. The son, confronted with a jumping guard, would have minuted him. This Toad *lectured* him, and lecturing is what a man does who has recently been handed something and wants it seen in his hand.

I could be wrong. I have written that in the margin in ink, not pencil, so that it does not rub out: *reading, not record.* If a second account arrives that puts the son in the new suit, the file moves and I say so. But I notice — and I am allowed to notice — that the Regency's whole defence of the father for fifteen years has been that his journal is a forgery and therefore he said none of it. The account does not come from his journal. It comes from a corridor, from a man who did not know who he was listening to and wrote down the one sentence a conspirator should never say out loud. *WAH! The Regency has spent a fortune proving a dead man did not write a page. It has not spent a coin proving he did not open a door.*

I leave the ruler where it is.

sections.heading: The Guild Was Not a Guest at the Meeting. The Guild Was the Clock
sections.sourceAnchor: *The guild is already in place.* And then: *we won't act yet.*
sections.body:
I have copied the night's six sentences onto one card in two columns, because I wanted to see them without the account's prose around them, and the card is in front of me propped against the lamp. Left column, the dungeon, three hoods: *the Guild is already in place; we won't act yet.* Right column, the hall, a Toad in a new suit: *like a lost dog; a nuisance to the Toads is a nuisance to us; Mages' Guild — dispatch of them.* Same night, an hour apart, a stair between them.

Read the grammar, not the drama. *In place* is a word for a mechanism. *We won't act yet* is a word for a date. A Guild that was joining a plot would say *we agree* or *we are with you*; this one said, in effect, *the installation is complete and the switch is not tonight.* The journal says *the Guild provided the method.* I had always read that as a potion, a spell, a thing handed over — and perhaps it was, perhaps it is in the fat vial — but the dungeon sentence says the method was not handed over. It was *installed.* The Guild did not give the Regency a tool. The Guild became the building's timing.

Now the right column, and I will give the last sentence its own line because it is the only one in the account that was said to an audience:

"Mages' Guild — dispatch of them."

That is an order. It is given in public, by the Toad with the keys, to the hoods a hall has just finished cheering, and a bolt follows it across the room. Set it beside *a nuisance to the Toads is a nuisance to us,* and look at the pronoun. *Us.* A Regency Toad, speaking of the Guild's interests as his own, or of his own as the Guild's — the sentence does not care which, and neither, that night, did anybody in the hall. The journal says *the Regency provided the opportunity.* I had read that as the date. It was also this: a man of the household, in front of witnesses, making a Guild killing a palace matter.

I turn the card over so I stop reading it. The Guild said *we won't act yet* in the dungeon and acted within the hour in the hall, and nobody in the account finds that contradictory, and I do not either. They did not act on the *plan.* They acted on a *Toad* — the one piece of the night that was not on the schedule — and they did it on the Chamberlain's say-so. *WAH! That is the whole Arrangement in one evening: the method waits, the opportunity speaks, and a lantern is the only thing they shoot at.*

sections.heading: Bowser Was the Only Honest Intruder in the Building, and They Charged Nothing to Put Him Down
sections.sourceAnchor: *He didn't know Fawful.* The Koopa King, a month before the Highsun 1 narrative made him Fawful's partner in the murder, stood in the ruins of a wall asking who that was.
sections.body:
The technology card for the orb is on the desk and it is mostly blank, which is unusual for me. *Small. Held up, not thrown. One. Pattern unknown.* I have written *pattern unknown* on a Guild entry before, but never one I had to write under a line that reads *to applause.*

Start with Bowser, because the account is kind to him in the way it is kind to the guard — by not knowing it should be. He came through a wall announcing himself. He said he had not been invited to the meeting, which is the most honest sentence any monarch says in this archive. He asked for the brothers; they were not there; he was disappointed. He asked to be taken to Peach. And when the bean's name was said in the smoke, he did not know it. A month later the kingdom would need him and Fawful on the same side of a door for the Highsun 1 narrative to hold, and here he is, a month early, standing in a wall he made, asking who Fawful is. Two intruders in one castle in one night is not a conspiracy. It is a coincidence somebody later found useful, and I would give a good deal to know how early *later* began. The Koopa in the shop says he alerted the castle to the attack. The castle *knew Bowser was coming.* Read it again: the only person surprised by Bowser that night was Bowser.

Now the orb, and here I have to pull a second file, because this is where the grievance lives. I cross to the shelf and take down the Guild invoice from the capital file — eight hundred and seventy gold, with three hundred of it for *compounding under duress,* a charge invented at a bench with an Archmage standing over it. I put it beside the orb card. In 1040 BF the Guild charges a party three hundred gold for making a potion while frightened. In 955 BF a hood put the Koopa King on the floor of Peach's Castle in one, with a fist-sized thing it has never shown anybody since, and did not send a bill. It took the applause instead. *WAH! I know what the Guild charges for help. I have the paper. The only thing it has ever done for free in this archive was the thing that made a hall of Toads love it, and the love is the invoice.*

The brothers walked in behind the cheering. Luigi tripped on a striped sock. I cannot source the sock and I have stopped trying; some things are in an account because they happened. What I can source is the order of events, and the order is the argument: Bowser down, Guild cheered, brothers late, guard shot at. Whoever wrote that schedule did not need the Mario brothers to be anywhere in particular. They needed them to be *busy,* and five hours later in a bean shop the Guild said so in those words.

I put the invoice back in its folder but leave the folder on the desk.

sections.heading: Nobody Said 'Trafficked' to Them. They Said It First
sections.sourceAnchor: *"Your son is being taken care of. Toad Lee won't have to worry about being trafficked in our care."*
sections.body:
I have to be careful here, so I will tell you where my hands are. The account is closed on the blotter. On the shelf behind me, three down from the Guild invoice, is a folder with Toad Lee's diary pages in it, and I have not taken it down, and I am not going to tonight. I am going to argue from the sentence alone.

The sentence was said to a father who had not yet asked. That is the first thing. He walked into a bean shop with a dead man's sword and a captain's sash on both arms and before he said *where is my son* they told him his son was being taken care of — which means they knew who he was before he came through the door, which means the letter in the dead guard's coat was not the only thing in that castle with the shop's address on it. The Guild had the boy and knew whose boy it was and had decided what to say about it before the father arrived. That is not protection. That is a *prepared statement.*

The second thing is the word. Nobody in that shop had said *trafficked.* The father had not said it; the account would have it if he had. The Guild volunteered it — put it into the room, attached to a small boy, in the negative, in the same breath as *our care* — and I have sat with that construction for most of an hour trying to find an innocent reason a person reaches for that word unprompted. I have not found one. You do not deny a thing nobody has accused you of unless the thing is in the room with you. I said in the filing that I would not editorialise on the sentence and I am keeping to it: I have put it on the record whole, and the people who said it chose the word, and that is the editorial.

And the third thing, which is mine. The boy at the long table past midnight with a plate in front of him is the Toad who sits across from me in 1040 and reads diaries on a shelf while stronger people argue about doors. I know him. I have filed him. I have never once asked him about 955 BF, and the account has just told me why I should and why I will not do it tonight. A boy who was *taken care of* by the Guild at that age grew up into a diplomat who lets other people shout. I had taken that for temperament. I am no longer sure it was not training.

The last line of the account is the Guild's, and the father's question that drew it was the right one — *escorts, to go and get him* — and the answer was: *"Are you stupid? You just said you don't trust us. We're protecting your son."* I read that as the Guild telling the truth for the only time in the night. He did not trust them. They had the boy. Both halves are correct and the sentence is built so that you cannot hold both at once. *WAH! That is not an insult. That is a lock.* The folder stays on the shelf.

sections.heading: A Bean in a Guild Cloak Explains an Edit I Have Never Understood
sections.sourceAnchor: *"Dispatch of this finkrat and takeover kingdom,"* Fawful said, in the Guild's cloak, and the two operatives did not correct the pronoun.
sections.body:
Last file. I reach down and pick the Who Signed folder up off the floor at last, because this is the part it is for, and I open it to the two drafts of Highsun 1 — the first, which named Fawful, and the second, which did not. I have had those two drafts side by side so many times that the corners are soft. Tonight, for the first time, I have a third sheet to put between them: a bean, in a Guild cloak, in his own shop, at dawn, saying *takeover kingdom* in the first person while two Guild operatives let him.

The cloak is the evidence, not the speech. Fawful says a great many things in capitals and the archive has learned to weigh them by the kilo. But the cloak was *given*. A Mages' Guild robe does not come off a peg in a bean shop; somebody in the Guild handed it to him, and two Guild hands watched him put it on over the red and did not take it back. A month later, when the kingdom chose its murderer, it chose the Koopa who had come through a wall shouting his own name and had never heard of the bean. It did not choose the bean. The first draft did. The second draft — the one that stuck — did not. I have asked for fifteen years who made that edit and why. Here is a why: by the time anyone was choosing, Fawful was wearing the Guild, and you do not hang a man in your own cloak.

I do not want to oversell the mushroom, so let me be exact about what the account gives and what it does not. The vacuum shroom is *described*: Fawful's own make, inhaled, turns the inhaler into a vacuum — Bowser breathes it, Bowser takes in everything in reach, brothers included — and the wards still being up was said as a problem by somebody and as a detail by Fawful. The fat vial is *named*: a glass thing with weight in it, the Koopa's, the dose's road into Bowser. Neither is *seen used*. I have put both on the technology ledger as exactly that and not a word further, and I would ask the reader to notice that the plan requires the Koopa King to be awake and screaming under the castle, which the shop reported he was, and which the Guild said was *the point*. Bowser was not the Arrangement's partner. Bowser was its *engine*, and a bean in a borrowed cloak was explaining how to fuel it.

I close the folder on the three sheets together and put it back on the floor, because the desk is still full. *WAH! Fifteen years to learn that the first draft was the honest one, from a shopkeeper with a borrowed coat.*

verdict:
Here is what is on the desk when I stop, and what I conclude from each piece.

The night posting, on top: a named guard on a named post at a named hour, a month before the journal's *positions were cleared.* That is the schedule's first line, and the Arrangement has one now instead of a disputed page. **The capital file takes this night as its first witnessed session**, and the leads it opens are the ones I want worked in this order: the fat vial, because it is the only object in the account that moved from the castle to the shop and has not been opened; the dispatch order, because a Chamberlain gave the Guild a killing in public and the Regency has never had to answer for a thing said out loud; and the dead guard's address, because a palace Toad in the hall was carrying directions to the bean shop and that means the shop had people above stairs as well as below.

The account, under it: a witness, not a verdict, and I have handled it as the file handles every 955 paper. It confirms the journal where the journal can be confirmed — the positions, the method, the opportunity — and it goes past the journal in one place the journal could not: it was heard by nobody's partisan. The attribution of the man in the new suit is **mine**, it is marked as mine in ink, and it moves the moment a second account moves it.

The Guild invoice, out of its folder: the orb cost nothing and bought a hall. That is the night's real transaction and the one I recommend the party understand before it pays the Guild another coin — in 1040 the Guild still sells help, and the account says what the Guild does with gratitude once it has it.

And the folder on the shelf that I did not take down. The boy at the long table is the Toad who reads at my table. I recommend nothing to the party about him. I recommend to myself that I ask, in daylight, with the account closed, and that I accept whatever answer a diplomat gives who learned very young that a room full of adults can be wrong at once. The schedule forgot the father. I do not think it forgot the son.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Two questions the account raises and cannot answer, laid against the plans and the paper the archive already holds. Nothing here changes the record; a sharpened guess at best, an honest wall at worst.

rolls.title: Was the hood in the corridor one of the three in the dungeon?
rolls.prompt: Walk the guard's route on the castle plans against the clock: the hood passed him between the dining hall and the tower, heading back toward the ceremonial route, and three hoods entered the dungeon behind Fawful some time after two guards had walked him down from the tower. Does the geometry allow one figure to be both?
rolls.success: It allows it, but only by the service stair behind the dining hall — the one that drops to the kitchens and then to the dungeon passage without touching the ceremonial route. A hood going *that* way was not heading for the dungeon when the guard saw it; it was coming *from* the direction of the stair, toward the hall where the captain would later stand, and it turned round. I read a runner: somebody checked the hall, found the brothers not yet there, and went back down to report that the meeting was late. The Guild in the dungeon knew the brothers had not arrived before Bowser did. That is a timing, not a name, and I file it as a timing.
rolls.failure: The plans do not resolve it. The account gives no time for the corridor and the dungeon passage has two approaches, one of which I have never had drawn. What survives is the limit itself: the castle's own plans do not show how the Guild moved between the dungeon and the hall, which means either my plans are short a stair or the Guild's route was not on anybody's plan. Both are worth knowing. Neither is a finding.

rolls.title: Was the dead guard going to the bean shop, or coming from it?
rolls.prompt: The letter in the dead Toad's livery reads *meet me in Fawful's bean shop* with no signature the account records. Set it against the night posting, which fixes the hall detail's hours, and against the five hours the drains took a lantern. Could a hall guard have been to Toad Town and back inside his posting?
rolls.success: Not by the drains and not on foot, which means the letter was *delivered* to him in the castle, that night or earlier, by somebody who could move paper from a Toad Town bean shop into palace livery — and the only people in the account moving freely between the two addresses are the Koopa, who was in the shop before the guard, and the Guild, who had the boy there by dawn. A hall guard with the shop's address on his body was a hall guard who had been *invited.* I count at least one Toad in the captain's own detail who was expected at the Bean Badge, and I note that he died in Bowser's fire standing where the captain stood, which the schedule did not plan either.
rolls.failure: The posting fixes the hours of the ceremonial route, not the hall, and I cannot put the dead Toad on a roster I do not hold. The letter stays what the account made it: an address on a body, unsigned, undated. The honest note is that the shop's reach into the castle is proven by the letter's existence and not by its route, and I should stop trying to make one sheet of paper do two jobs.
